name: Norfolk Island pines of Praça da República

location.address: Jardim da Praça da República, Horta, Faial, Azores

official_register.name: Património Classificado dos Açores: Exemplares Arbóreos (Governo dos Açores, DRC/SRAAC), CC BY 4.0

access: Free; municipal square garden in the centre of Horta (owner: Câmara Municipal da Horta per the register), open public square
transport: Central Horta, 2 minutes on foot from the Mercado Municipal; about 5 minutes from the marina
story:
These three conifers come from one small island in the South Pacific, between New Zealand and New Caledonia, the only place on earth where the species grows wild. Norfolk Island pines are not true pines at all. They are araucarias, cousins of the monkey puzzle, and they grow like no native Azorean tree does. Each has one straight trunk, with branches set in flat, evenly spaced tiers, as if someone had drawn a tree with a ruler.

They have stood in Horta's main square long enough to be written into law. On 1 September 1984 the Azores listed all three in the annex of the regional decree that protects the town's notable trees, and Horta's own regulation of 2023 lists them again, with the municipality as their owner. Both documents say what the trees are and where. Neither says how tall they are, how thick, or who planted them.

The visit is short and free. The garden of Praça da República is an open public square in the centre of town, two minutes from the market and five from the marina. One pine stands on the square's east side; the other two stand about 35 metres to the west. Count them when you arrive. The region's own list notes that each tree's exact position still needs checking on the ground, so if you find two, or four, tell us.

Nobody has published an age for these trees. If you know when they went in, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by their shape, one straight trunk with branches in flat, even tiers. Three stand in the square's garden, one on its east side and two about 35 metres west of it.

name: Dragon trees of Jardim Florêncio Terra

location.address: Jardim Florêncio Terra, Horta, Faial, Azores

official_register.name: Património Classificado dos Açores: Exemplares Arbóreos (Governo dos Açores, DRC/SRAAC), CC BY 4.0

access: Free; municipal public garden (Jardim Florêncio Terra, owner Câmara Municipal da Horta per the register and regulation), opening hours not published in the sources read
transport: Central Horta, about 5 minutes on foot from the Praça da República
story:
Five dragon trees stand in one compact garden in the centre of Horta, all inside a patch about 45 metres by 40.

A dragon tree is barely a tree. It is a monocot, closer kin to asparagus and agave than to any oak, and it lays down no annual rings. It grows slowly, branches only after it flowers, and so builds its crown by forking, then forking again, until the trunk carries an umbrella of stiff, sword-shaped leaves. Its resin dries dark red, the dragon's blood traded for centuries as a dye and a medicine. None of these grew wild on Faial. They were planted here as garden specimens.

They were already worth protecting in 1984, when the annex of a regional decree of 1 September listed the dragon trees of Jardim Florêncio Terra among Horta's notable trees. The two official lists do not agree on how many there are. The region's geodata marks five points in the garden; the town's 2023 regulation lists fewer. Count them and tell us which is right. The garden also holds a protected Norfolk Island pine, the same species as the three in Praça da República, five minutes' walk away.

Entry is free. Opening hours are not published, so allow for a closed gate early or late in the day.

No source gives an age for any of the five, and without rings a dragon tree keeps its age to itself. If you know when they were planted, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by their crowns, branches forking again and again into tufts of stiff, sword-shaped leaves. Five stand within about 45 metres of each other. The tall tiered conifer near them is the garden's Norfolk Island pine.
